variants.name: tokio CancellationToken + task handles (async)
variants.implementation_notes: In async Rust the two phases are a token and a join: CancellationToken::cancel() is phase 1 (one-way, wakes every waiter; cancelled() is a future to select on, child_token() scopes it), and awaiting the JoinHandle/JoinSet/TaskTracker is phase 2 - tokio's shutdown guide puts the cleanup (flush data, send a final message) inside the task before it returns, then waits for the tasks to finish. The classic structure (an atomic flag plus join) survives in synchronous code, where std::thread gives you join but no stop primitive at all.
pitfalls: A token is one-way and shared by its clones: reusing a cancelled token for new work cancels it immediately, so derive a child_token per generation.

Dropping a JoinSet aborts its tasks (the docs say so), and JoinSet::shutdown()/abort_all deliberately skip cleanup: keep the handles and await them, and put anything that must survive in a Drop guard or a shutdown path that runs before the next await.

Cancellation is observed only at await points: a long synchronous block or a std::thread::sleep inside a task ignores the token entirely (move such work to spawn_blocking and give it its own stop signal).
A panic in the task skips the rest of its body, including a hand-written flush; cleanup that must run regardless belongs in Drop.

variants.name: std threads: Arc<AtomicBool> + join
variants.implementation_notes: Rust's standard library has no cancellation: std::thread gives you a handle and join, so the pattern is rebuilt from an Arc<AtomicBool> latch (store with Release, load with Acquire when the flag guards published data), a channel receive with timeout or a Condvar so the worker wakes and re-checks, and JoinHandle::join() as the completion step (its Result also surfaces a panic as phase 2's failure). Cleanup runs after the loop because a dropped closure cannot run async code; if the worker owns resources that must be released even on panic, wrap them in Drop guards.
pitfalls: Detaching (dropping the JoinHandle) removes the only way to know the thread finished - Rust programmes have no other completion signal, so keep the handle and join with a bound.
A blocking recv() without timeout hides the flag; use recv_timeout, a self-pipe, or a Condvar with a predicate so the request is actually observed.
Relaxed ordering is only safe when nothing else depends on the flag; publishing data before a Release store and reading after an Acquire load is what makes the cleanup visible to the joiner.
A panicking worker unwinds without running explicit cleanup code: RAII drops still run, but a hand-written flush at the end of the loop does not.
